name: CPU Profiling & Flame Graphs
tagline: Statistical 99 Hz stack sampling with <2% overhead, folded into proportional Flame Graphs that expose self-time plateaus and inclusive hotspots.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of CPU profiling and Flame Graphs—from avoiding observer-effect instrumentation and lockstep aliasing to Differential Flame Graphs in production.

spark.summary: Sampling CPU profilers capture call stacks at fixed intervals (e.g., 99 Hz) with <1% overhead, and Flame Graphs aggregate those stacks into proportional width rectangles so hot code paths jump out immediately.
spark.keyTakeaway: Flame Graphs measure inclusive time on the horizontal axis—not chronological time—so wide plateaus reveal where your CPU actually spends cycles, even when scattered across thousands of calls.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Instrumenting every function entry/exit distorts timings by 10x–100x (the **observer effect**) and misses kernel/libc time.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts 99 Hz Linux perf Capture -> Stack Collapse -> Flame Graph (PMU Timer (99Hz) -> Kernel Unwind -> stackcollapse -> Flame Graph); Flame Graph Hierarchy (Inclusive Base -> Self-Time Plateau) (main -> handle_req -> parse_json (61.5%) -> verify_sig (38.5%) -> serde::from_slice).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choose the profiler that understands your runtime's stack frames and avoids safepoint bias. Continuous profilers (Parca, Pyroscope, Cloud Profiler) run eBPF/runtime samplers as a DaemonSet at 19–99 Hz, uploading collapsed stacks every 10–60s so teams can generate.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Connect CPU profiling with Linux CFS throttling, Python GIL contention, JVM memory behavior, and off-CPU distributed tracing.

learningJourney.title: What are Sampling Profilers & Flame Graphs
learningJourney.explanation:
Instrumenting every function entry/exit distorts timings by 10x–100x (the **observer effect**) and misses kernel/libc time. **Statistical sampling profilers** (`perf`, `async-profiler`, `pprof`, `py-spy`) interrupt each CPU core at a fixed rate (e.g., **99 Hz**) via kernel timers or PMUs, record the instruction pointer and call stack with <2% overhead, and resume.

A **Flame Graph** folds identical call stacks together: the **Y-axis** is call-stack depth (bottom = root, top = leaf executing on CPU) and the **X-axis** is sorted alphabetically by frame name—where **box width** equals the percentage of total samples containing that frame.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Statistical Sampling & Flame Graphs
learningJourney.explanation: Without sampling + visual stack folding, megabytes of raw stack traces hide systemic bottlenecks like repeated regex compilation, JSON deserialization, or JVM GC safepoint tax.

learningJourney.title: Where On-CPU Profiling Works (and When to Use Off-CPU)
learningJourney.explanation: On-CPU sampling only fires when a core is actively executing instructions. If CPU is 10% and p99 latency is 500 ms, threads are sleeping on I/O, DNS, or mutexes.

comparison.choice: Use: High CPU Utilization & Regression Diffs
benefits: Captures hot loops, serialization, GC mark/sweep, and syscall overhead at <2% prod cost.
costs: Normalizes to 100% of captured samples—always check total CPU% first.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Blocked I/O, Mutex Waits & Sleep Stalls
benefits: Switch to eBPF `offcputime` or OpenTelemetry distributed tracing instead.
costs: On-CPU samplers are completely blind to threads parked in `epoll_wait` or `futex`.

benefits: Use hardware PMU counters (`perf stat`) or `JMH` / `criterion`.
costs: 10 ms sampling period is 1,000,000x coarser than nanosecond functions.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How to Capture Clean Stacks & Read Plateaus
learningJourney.explanation:
1. **Preserve Frame Pointers**: Compile C/C++/Rust with `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` so kernel unwinding takes ~100 ns without `[unknown]` towers.
2. **Generate JIT Maps**: Use `async-profiler` on JVM (no safepoint bias) and `--perf-basic-prof` on Node.js/V8.
3. **Read Two Shapes**: **Wide flat plateaus** at the top = self-time hotspots (`serde_json::from_slice`); **wide towers with thin spires** = high inclusive time from calling tiny helpers in a loop.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```bash
# Capture 30s at 99 Hz with frame-pointer unwinding, collapse, and diff against baseline
perf record -F 99 -a -g --call-graph fp -- sleep 30
perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > new.folded
flamegraph.pl new.folded > cpu.svg

# Differential Flame Graph (red = CPU regression, blue = speedup)
difffolded.pl baseline.folded new.folded | flamegraph.pl > diff.svg
```

comparison.choice: C / C++ / Rust: Linux `perf` (FP vs DWARF)
costs: DWARF unwinding (`--call-graph dwarf`) copies 8 KB stack/sample (5–15% overhead).
Avoid `jstack`/JVMTI samplers, which blame safepoints instead of tight loops.

benefits: <1% overhead at 100 Hz; built-in HTTP endpoint.
costs: Excludes Cgo/kernel frames unless paired with `perf` or eBPF.
Pass `--native` to correlate C-extension frames (NumPy, Cython).
